description: We’re students at the Muhammad al-Khwarizmi IT school in Tashkent who like building things that mix code and hardware. We work in C++, C#, Python, Java and SQL, plus Unity, FlutterFlow, Arduino and Blender. Our projects include Bytez, an eco app/game with 3D worlds for Technovation Girls, and a climate control system with sensors, C++ firmware and a 3D-printed case. We’ve done hackathons together, so we know how to ship something that works under a tight deadline.
summary:
Outpost Zero is an educational 16-bit pixel-art strategy game and space habitat simulator that puts players in the role of NASA mission architects. To address the challenge of making space mission design engaging and accessible, the game guides players through real engineering trade studies to sustain a 4-person crew for 5 to 100 days under strict mass (35t) and budget ($500M) constraints.
Players choose from 9 celestial targets and 27 real-world locations—including the Lunar South Pole, Jezero Crater, Venusian 50km cloud cities (HAVOC), Europa, and Titan’s Selk Crater—each modeled on NASA data (LCROSS, SWIM, Fission Surface Power, Dragonfly) for solar illumination, water ice deposits, and radiation levels. Players then assemble four core subsystems: Energy (solar arrays, batteries, or a 6t 40kW nuclear reactor), Life Support (Earth supplies, closed-loop ECLSS recycling, or ISRU ice mining), Radiation Shielding (light frame, regolith cover, multilayer shield), and Comms.
During the day-by-day survival simulation, players manage Energy, Water, Oxygen, Crew Health, and Science while surviving 14-day lunar nights, Martian dust storms, solar flares, and airlock leaks, concluding with a detailed engineering debrief.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Outpost Zero is a pixel-art browser game in which the player designs and runs a crewed base anywhere in the Solar System. The player picks a destination (Moon, Mars, Mercury, Venus, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune, or an Earth training analog), then chooses a site such as the lunar south pole, Titan’s Selk crater, or a floating platform in Jupiter’s clouds, since a gas giant has no surface to land on. Each site has its own light, ice, and radiation levels. With a fixed mass and budget, the player picks power, life support, radiation shielding, and communications. Not everything fits, so every choice is a trade-off.

The ship then flies across an animated map of the Solar System. Flight time grows with real distance, and the route to the outer planets crosses the asteroid belt as an optional piloting mini-game. At the base, a live scene shows events such as air leaks, meteor showers, solar flares, dust storms, and frost. Bad decisions damage modules, which leak resources every day until they are repaired. If energy, water, oxygen, or crew health runs out, the screen shows GAME OVER and the cause. Each world has a science goal, Mission Control comments over the radio, and a final report explains what went wrong.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Players do a simplified version of what NASA engineers call a trade study: comparing options by mass, cost, power, and risk. They learn why solar panels fail far from the Sun, why radiation shielding matters, and why missions are so hard and expensive. Kids aged 5 to 12 get a brighter theme with less text. The game is available in English, Uzbek, and Russian, so students in Uzbekistan can learn in their own language.

NASA DATA

Key values come from NASA sources linked inside the game: the Fission Surface Power reactor target (40 kW, under 6 t), Curiosity RAD radiation on Mars, the Chang’e 4 lunar dose (published research, not NASA), MESSENGER polar ice on Mercury, SWIM ice maps for Arcadia Planitia, the HAVOC concept for Venus, the HOPE study for a Callisto base, Dragonfly’s Titan landing site, Voyager 2 data for Miranda and Triton, the NASA Planetary Fact Sheet, and NASA analog missions on Earth. Numbers are simplified for gameplay, and the game says so openly.

TOOLS

HTML5, CSS3, and plain JavaScript with no frameworks, all in one file that works offline. Pixel art is drawn from code with SVG and Canvas 2D. Chiptune music and sound effects are generated live with the Web Audio API. Player profiles and medals are saved in the browser with localStorage. Fonts: GNU Unifont and Press Start 2P, both open-source. An AI assistant (Claude) helped with code review, fact-checking, and translations. The game design and decisions are ours.

CREATIVITY

Every playthrough is different: the destination, site, modules, mission length (5 to 100 days), and daily decisions all change the outcome. Damage stays on the base and must be repaired, meteor craters remain on the ground, and the game reacts to each decision.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Scientific honesty (sources, and clear notes where values are estimates), accessibility for different ages and languages, privacy (a child’s age is never sent anywhere), and keeping the screen readable with less text and clear pixel fonts.
